name: fixes
_comment: A/B of the 2026-09-07 record-cache fixes, as an in-campaign comparison.
Three SUTs, ONE amalgamation each, same driver, same flags:
stock   upstream SQLite (-DSQLITE_OMIT_BF_CACHE)
bf_pre  BF built from src/ at the revision passed to
`build_suts.sh --pre REV` -- i.e. BEFORE the fixes
bf      BF built from the current working tree -- AFTER them
Why bf_pre exists at all: identical code measured in three separate
campaigns reported 9913 / 11652 / 8102 ops/s (23% spread), so a
before/after read off two results directories is not evidence. The
'before' has to run interleaved with the 'after', under the same cgroup,
the same page-cache state and the same governor.
This config is deliberately NOT strict: the fixes are uncommitted, so the
tree is dirty by construction, and the governor is powersave unless you
run the sudo line in the README. Both are recorded in the manifest and
printed as caveats. Wall-clock ratios here are therefore weaker evidence
than the counters (ring MiB, buffered%, evictions, frames/commit), which
are governor-independent.
Each experiment names the fix it interrogates. ~110 runs, budget ~1.5 h.
Two reading rules for the bf_pre rows (README section 10):
- counters newer than the pre revision come back absent, not zero, and its
`rec hit%` is the old conflated page+record counter -- not comparable;
- bf_pre ignores the ring resize, so its ring is 8 MiB whatever the budget
says and it runs UNDER budget. Under a cgroup that also caps the page
cache, the engine holding less anon memory gets more file cache for free,
which flatters it. That is why every experiment below names a counter to
read before the wall clock.

experiments.name: cache_size
_tests: FIX 3 -- PRAGMA bf_cache_size never took effect: the cache is
built during the schema load, always before the BF pragmas can
run, so the ring stayed at its 8 MiB default for every run ever
measured. Isolated on a fully-cached 2M-row zipf read the fix
The prediction this experiment can falsify: bf_pre is FLAT
across the axis (its ring is 8 MiB at every budget) while bf
scales with it. Read `ring MiB` in the detail table first -- if
bf_pre is not flat at 8, the diagnosis was wrong.
memmax is auto (2x budget + 256M): a fixed cap turns a cache-size
axis into a page-cache-eviction axis.

experiments.name: promotion
_tests: THE OPEN PROBLEM. Read-path promotion costs ~20% at the real
256 MiB ring (it was 20.1% -> 3.8% after the size-class fix ->
20.1% again once the ring became real). Suspected cause is in
sqlite3BfCircularBufferAlloc: freed blocks return to a size-class
free list but do NOT return logical ring space, so the ring holds
~3.8 KiB per ~130 B record and every upgrade burns space until
the head sweeps past. `cached recs` and `evictions` at
promotion=100 are the columns to read; ops/s is downstream of them.

experiments.name: scan
_tests: Fixes 1+2 change how many records a mini-page holds, so a scan
that merges buffered records with base pages should see it. Also
the paper's ~2.5x scan claim, for reference.

experiments.name: negative_read
_tests: Recorded as ~4.5x SLOWER than stock while reading 5x fewer bytes
-- a CPU-bound path, the opposite of the paper's 5.6 phantom-cache
claim. Included to find out whether the size-class fixes moved it
at all; if the ratio is unchanged, the cause is elsewhere and this
stops being attributable to mini-page sizing.

experiments.name: record_size
_tests: FIX 2 -- the documented '64-96 byte cliff'. sqlite3BfRecordWrite
upgraded one size class per write, so a mini-page starting at 64 B
reached only 128 B, whose usable payload is 128-24(hdr)-8(meta) =
96 bytes; anything larger fell back to the base-page path (100%
buffered at 64 B, 31% at 96 B, 14% at 200 B). Fixed by
sqlite3BfMiniPageSizeClassFor(), which picks the smallest class
holding the live records plus the incoming one, so one upgrade
always suffices.
Read `buffered%`: bf_pre should collapse from ~100 at v32/v64 to
~14 at v200, bf should stay high. This is the clearest single
before/after in the whole config. value_len is a property of the
loaded table, so each point needs its own dataset.

experiments.name: update
_tests: UPDATE was measured never to buffer at all (wal_record_frames=0,
buffered_inserts=0) and to take the page-image path instead. The
size-class fixes plausibly change that, since refusing a record
for want of space was one of the reasons. `rec frames/commit` > 0
for bf and = 0 for bf_pre would be the signal.
On v100, not big: write runs copy the database per run, and a
6.8 GB copy per repeat dominates a 30 s measurement.

experiments.name: write_amp
_tests: The Phase-2 commit claim -- 1 page frame per commit, ~30x less
WAL than stock with group commit -- at a 100 B record rather than
the 64 B payload wal_write_amp.sh used, which was exactly the size
where buffering always succeeded. Read `WAL B/commit stock/bf`.
